p.title: How a scientific idea improves
p.challenge: Press Next. At the question, choose "No" to see how science changes when new evidence appears

nodes.text: Scientists hold an idea based on evidence
nodes.info: Long ago many people believed the Earth was the centre of everything.
The telescope and the microscope let people see things they could never see before.

nodes.text: Does the new evidence fit the idea?
nodes.info: Scientific ideas stand or fall on evidence, not on opinion or age.
Keep the idea, keep checking it. An idea that fits all the evidence is kept, but scientists go on testing it.
Scientists test and check the new evidence carefully. Scientists repeat observations to be sure they are right.
Improve or replace the idea. Careful observations showed that the Earth and the planets go around the Sun. In 2006, Pluto was placed in a new group: dwarf planets.
Every answer leads to new questions. Science is never finished, so it keeps growing.

p.title: Inquiry: finding out step by step
p.challenge: Meena wants to know if salt makes ice melt faster. Arrange her inquiry steps in order

nodes.info: Curiosity starts with noticing something.

nodes.text: Ask: does salt make ice melt faster?
nodes.info: A question you can test.
A guess that a test can check.
Plan a fair test with two ice cubes. Same size of cube, same place, same time. Only one cube gets salt.
Is ONLY the salt different? In a fair test you change only one thing. Salt in the sun and no salt in the shade is NOT fair.
Do the test and record what really happens. Write down the true result, even if it surprises you.
Repeating shows the result is not just luck.
Does the result support the hypothesis?

p.title: Metal or non-metal?
p.challenge: Use lustre, malleability, ductility and sound to sort each material. Watch out for the tricky ones!

items.why: Metals are malleable: aluminium is beaten into thin foil.
Silver is a malleable metal; vark is a very thin sheet of it.
Metals are ductile: copper is drawn into thin wires.
Sulphur is brittle: it breaks into powder when hammered.
Coal is brittle and dull: a non-metal.
Mercury is a metal that is liquid at room temperature.
Sodium is a metal, but so soft it can be cut with a knife.
Iodine is shiny, but it is a non-metal — an exception.
Graphite conducts electricity, but it is a non-metal — an exception.

p.title: Will this iron nail rust?
p.challenge: Nail A is in dry air, nail B is in boiled water under oil, nail C is in a little water open to air. Press Next and answer for each nail

nodes.info: Nail A is kept with a drying agent, so it has no moisture.
Nail B: boiling removes air from the water and the oil layer stops new air getting in.
Rust is a reddish-brown substance, iron oxide. Iron + oxygen + water → rust. This is a chemical change; rust flakes off and fresh iron below rusts too.
Without either air or water, iron does not rust.
Paint, oil or grease, galvanise (coat with zinc) or use stainless steel. These keep air and water away from the iron.

nodes.text: Friends push Rohan to try gutkha

nodes.info: Tobacco, alcohol and drugs harm the growing body and brain.
Good friends respect your no. Real friends do not push you into harm.
He moves away from the group.
He talks to a trusted adult. A parent, a teacher or a school counsellor can help.

panels: The end in the flame gets hot first
Heat passes to the part just next to the flame
Then the middle of the rod gets hot
Last of all, the far end gets hot

p.title: Conduction, convection or radiation?
p.challenge: How does the heat travel in each case? Sort them all, then press Check.

items.text: Steel ladle handle gets hot in dal
items.why: Heat passes particle to particle while the steel stays in place: conduction.

items.text: Water circulating in a heated pan
items.why: Warm water rises and cooler water sinks: a convection current.

items.text: Warm air rising from a stove
items.why: Warm air is lighter and rises: convection.

items.text: Hot air leaving by a high ventilator
items.why: Warm air rises and goes out from high up: convection.

items.text: The Sun's heat reaching the Earth
items.why: It crosses empty space with no material in between: radiation.

items.text: Warmth on your face in front of a fire
items.why: We feel radiation from a fire or heater.

items.text: Black solar panel getting hot in sunlight
items.why: Dark surfaces absorb more of the Sun's radiation.

nodes.info: Land heats up faster than the sea.
Air above the hot land warms and rises.
Cooler air from over the sea moves in towards the land.
Land cools down faster than the sea.
Air above the warmer sea rises.
Cooler air from the land moves out to the sea.

p.title: What gas does a plant give out?
p.challenge: Plants respire day and night. Press Next and choose Day or Night to see which gas the plant gives out

nodes.text: Every living part of the plant respires
nodes.info: Roots, stems, leaves, flowers and seeds break down food using oxygen to release energy.
Photosynthesis AND respiration happen. Photosynthesis makes more oxygen than the plant uses.
The plant gives out OXYGEN.
Only respiration happens. With no light there is no photosynthesis.
The plant gives out carbon dioxide.

p.title: How much light passes through?
p.challenge: Sort each material: does it let almost all light, some light or no light through?

items.why: Clear glass lets almost all light through.
Clean water lets almost all light through.
Butter paper lets some light through: translucent.
Frosted glass lets only some light through.
Wood lets no light through, so it casts a shadow.
Cardboard blocks light: opaque.
Your body is opaque — that is how shadow puppets work.

p.title: Solar eclipse or lunar eclipse?
p.challenge: Sort each fact under the eclipse it describes, then press Check.

items.text: Moon comes between Sun and Earth
items.why: In a solar eclipse the Moon is in the middle.

items.text: Moon's shadow falls on the Earth
items.why: The Moon blocks the Sun, so its shadow falls on the Earth.

items.text: Can happen only on a new moon day
items.why: Only at new moon is the Moon between the Sun and the Earth.
Never look at the Sun directly, even during a solar eclipse.

items.text: Earth comes between Sun and Moon
items.why: In a lunar eclipse the Earth is in the middle.

items.text: Earth's shadow falls on the Moon
items.why: The Earth blocks sunlight from reaching the Moon.

items.text: Can happen only on a full moon night
items.why: Only at full moon is the Earth between the Sun and the Moon.
In a total lunar eclipse the Moon often looks reddish.

items.text: Safe to watch with bare eyes
items.why: A lunar eclipse is safe to watch without glasses.
